title: How Diffusion Models Memorize
claim: Memorized and normal generations separate measurably at each denoising step, and empirical quantities match the theoretical predictions of each theorem.
layout: 6 panels, 2x3 grid, each captioned with its theorem number
description: A 2x3 grid of line and scatter plots, each captioned with a theorem number: (a) Thm. 1, (b) Thm. 2, (c) Thm. 3, (d) Thm. 4, (e) Thm. 5, (f) Thm. 8. Coral curves mark memorized prompts (SSCD > 0.7) and dark purple curves mark normal prompts, each with a shaded band for spread. Panels (a) and (c) show falling tail-probability curves against a normalized radius. Panel (a) also has hatched forward-latent curves. Panel (b) is a single teal curve rising against alpha-bar on a log axis. Panel (d) shows the coral and purple curves separated across denoising steps. Panel (e) is a scatter along the y=x diagonal, with points colored by SSCD on a magma-like colorbar. Panel (f) shows a decaying difference norm, higher for memorized prompts. Axis labels carry dense math notation.
caption: Denoising measurements on SDv1 (DDIM). Coral and purple in (a,c,d,f) denote memorized and normal prompt groups, respectively ([ref]). In (a), dashed and solid curves correspond to forward latents and Gaussian initializations, respectively. In (a--c,f), curves show means across prompts, and shaded bands indicate $\pm1$ standard deviation. Seeds are first averaged within each prompt in (b,f). In (d), curves and shaded bands show the median and interquartile range, respectively, with each prompt receiving equal total weight. In (e), point colors indicate each generated image's final SSCD, and the dotted diagonal denotes equality.
abstract: Despite their success in image generation, diffusion models can unintentionally memorize and reproduce training data, raising serious privacy and copyright concerns. Although prior work has studied memorization from different perspectives, a unified account of how this reproduction occurs during generation remains incomplete. In this paper, we develop a mathematical account of this process in text-to-image latent diffusion models with classifier-free guidance. We trace reproduction across denoising steps through predictions of the final denoised latent made with and without the prompt. Assuming these predictions are Bayes-optimal and uniformly bounded, we show that sufficiently low loss on a training prompt--image pair enables the prediction made with the prompt to reproduce the paired training latent with high probability, even at the first denoising step. At this first step, we bound the difference between the prediction made without the prompt and the empirical mean of the training latents, showing how guidance amplifies the reproduced training latent's deviation from that mean. We then quantify how the latent passed between denoising steps carries prompt influence to subsequent predictions made without the prompt. When both predictions are sufficiently close to the paired training latent at the final step, their guided combination also reproduces it in the final generated latent. We also analyze how their difference evolves, showing that closer agreement alone does not establish reproduction. Finally, our account provides a unified explanation of existing detection and mitigation strategies.
